notes:
Now let me compile the verse-by-verse notes from all the material I've gathered:

---

# John 16 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

---

## v. 1 — "I have told you these things so that you will not fall away."

**Traditional Reading:** Jesus' motive in forewarning the disciples is pastoral: He wants to prevent them from being "scandalised" — caught off guard like an animal in a trap. The Greek verb *skandalizō* derives from *skandalon*, the spring-loaded stick in a trap that snaps shut unexpectedly (Tasker, cited in both Enduring Word and Precept Austin). Jesus previously warned of the world's hatred (John 15:18–25); now He explains why He told them. Gill notes that hardships arriving unannounced "bear the harder upon their spirits" and that forewarning prevents stumbling and abandoning one's profession of faith.

- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-16/ — "Jesus warned His disciples of coming opposition because He did not want them to be surprised and stumbled by it."
- **Precept Austin:** https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-16-commentary — Collects Spurgeon, Tasker, Dods, and Robertson on *skandalizō*; the NET Note adds that the verb means "to trip up disciples and cause them to fall away from Jesus' company."
- **Gill (Baptist, older):** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/john/16.htm — "His view in speaking of them, was not to discourage them, but to prevent their stumbling at them."
- **Ellicott (Anglican, older):** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/16.htm — "He had foretold them of the hatred of the world and also of the witness of the Spirit."

**Denominational differences:** No major disagreement. All traditions see the verse as pastoral forewarning to prevent apostasy under persecution. The Calvinist/Reformed reading (hinted at in Spurgeon via Precept Austin) adds that God's sovereign care ensures believers will persevere, but forewarning is the means He uses.

---

## v. 2 — "They will put you out of the synagogues. In fact, a time is coming when anyone who kills you will think he is offering a service to God."

**Traditional Reading:** "Put out of the synagogues" (*aposynagōgos*) refers to formal excommunication from Jewish worship. Gill, drawing on rabbinic sources, explains this was the greater excommunication (*Cherem* or *Shammatha*), cutting a person off from the whole Jewish community — not merely the lesser *Niddui*. The phrase "offers God service" translates *latreia* — the technical term for priestly sacrificial service. Barclay (cited by Guzik) notes it is "the normal word for the service that a priest rendered at the altar." Jesus thus predicts that religious zealots will regard murdering Christians as an act of worship. Ellicott cites a Rabbinic comment on Numbers 25:13: "Whosoever sheddeth the blood of the wicked is as he who offereth sacrifice." Both Gill and Ellicott point to Saul of Tarsus (Acts 26:9; Galatians 1:13–14) and the martyrdom of Stephen as early fulfilments.

- **Gill:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/john/16.htm
- **Ellicott:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/16.htm
- **Enduring Word (Guzik):** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-16/ — notes the 20th-century anomaly of atheistic communist persecution versus the historic pattern of religiously motivated persecution.

---

## v. 3 — "They will do these things because they have not known the Father or Me."

**Traditional Reading:** The root cause of religious persecution is ignorance of God — not mere intellectual ignorance but wilful failure to recognise God as He has revealed Himself in Christ. Ellicott makes the pastoral point: "They can know nothing of the true nature of the living Father who pitieth every child, and willeth not the death of a sinner." Gill notes this is mentioned "not to extenuate or excuse their sin" but as an argument for the disciples to bear ill usage with patience and to pray for their persecutors (as Christ prayed, "Father, forgive them, they know not what they do").

- **Ellicott:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/16.htm
- **Gill:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/john/16.htm — "Their zeal was not according to knowledge, it was a blind and misguided one."

---

## v. 4 — "But I have told you these things so that when their hour comes, you will remember that I told you about them. I did not tell you these things from the beginning, because I was with you."

**Traditional Reading:** Jesus repeats the purpose of forewarning (cf. v. 1). "Their hour" refers to the appointed time of persecution. Remembering Jesus' prediction would confirm His omniscience, strengthen faith, and encourage endurance. The reason He did not speak this way earlier ("from the beginning") is that while He was physically present, the world's hatred was directed at Him, not the disciples; He bore the brunt of it Himself. As Tasker says, "as long as He was with them the world's hatred must inevitably be drawn to Himself." Dods adds: "While He was with them they leant upon Him and could not apprehend a time of weakness and persecution." Ellicott notes that this is not inconsistent with Matthew 10, where Jesus did warn of persecution — the difference is that only now does He give the *full* account including the Spirit's role and the principles behind the world's hatred, now that His bodily departure is imminent.

- **Enduring Word:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-16/
- **Precept Austin:** https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-16-commentary
- **Ellicott:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/16.htm
- **Gill:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/john/16.htm

---

## v. 5 — "Now, however, I am going to Him who sent Me; yet none of you asks Me, 'Where are You going?'"

**Traditional Reading:** Peter had asked "Lord, where are You going?" (John 13:36) and Thomas had raised a similar question (John 14:5). Therefore Jesus must mean something deeper: the *heart* of the question. The disciples asked only about what would happen *to themselves* when Jesus left, not out of loving interest in Jesus' own glorious destiny — His return to the Father. As Morris puts it (cited by Guzik), Peter "had been concerned with the thought of parting with Jesus, not with that of the Master's destination." Gill likewise notes Peter "had no notion of his going out of the world, or to heaven to his Father."

- **Enduring Word:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-16/
- **Ellicott:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/16.htm — "None of you are out of love for Me asking about the place whither I am going. Your thoughts are not with Me."

---

## v. 6 — "Instead, your hearts are filled with sorrow because I have told you these things."

**Traditional Reading:** Sorrow over Jesus' departure so filled the disciples' hearts that it left no room for curiosity about His glorious destination. Ellicott says: "The thought of their own separation from Him, and of the dark future which lay before them, so filled their hearts that it left room for no thoughts of Him." The disciples could only see loss; they could not yet see gain.

- **Enduring Word:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-16/
- **Ellicott:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/16.htm
- **Gill:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/john/16.htm

---

## v. 7 — "But I tell you the truth, it is for your benefit that I am going away. Unless I go away, the Advocate will not come to you; but if I go, I will send Him to you."

**Traditional Reading:** This is a staggering claim: Jesus' departure is not merely tolerable but *advantageous* (*sympherei*, "expedient"). Guzik draws out the paradox: "To your advantage that Jesus is arrested? Beaten? Nailed to a cross?" Yet the reason is that only through His death, resurrection, and ascension could the Holy Spirit be sent. The Spirit's universal presence is better than Jesus' bodily presence limited to one location. Alford (cited by Guzik) says: "The dispensation of the Spirit is a more blessed manifestation of God than was even the bodily presence of the risen Saviour." Dods: "The withdrawal of the bodily presence of Christ was the essential condition of His universal spiritual presence." Guzik lists five reasons the Spirit's presence is better: (1) Jesus can be with every believer everywhere; (2) believers can understand Jesus better through the completed Scriptures; (3) a more trusting faith-relationship is possible; (4) Jesus' enthronement clarifies His finished work; (5) the disciples' own transformation at Pentecost proves the point.

Gill adds a theological rationale: "If Christ had not gone away or died, there would have been nothing for the Spirit to have done; no blood to sprinkle; no righteousness to reveal."

**Reformed Reading (Piper, Desiring God):** Emphasises that the Spirit makes Christ's glory *more real* than physical presence could. Piper writes: "The Spirit is going to make the glory of Jesus more real. Yes, more real than if he were there in the flesh." https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/no-one-will-take-your-joy-from-you — and in a separate article Piper explains the Spirit convicts the world *through the church's witness*, which required Christ's finished work first: https://www.desiringgod.org/interviews/why-is-it-better-that-christ-went-away-john-16-7

- **Enduring Word:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-16/
- **Gill:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/john/16.htm
- **Ellicott:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/16.htm
- **Desiring God (Piper):** https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/no-one-will-take-your-joy-from-you

---

## vv. 8–11 — The Spirit's Convicting Work

**v. 8 — "And when He comes, He will convict the world in regard to sin and righteousness and judgment."**

**Traditional Reading:** The Greek verb *elegchō* has a broader meaning than the English "convict." It also means to expose, refute, convince (Bruce, cited by Guzik). Ellicott's preferred translation is "convince." Guzik explains the threefold work: "Sin is the truth about man, righteousness is the truth about God, judgment is the inevitable combination of these two truths." The Spirit acts as "counsel for the prosecution" (Bruce) toward the unbelieving world, while being the Advocate for believers. Alford says each person's conscience already has "some glimmering" in these three areas, but the Spirit makes them real and practical. The first great historical fulfilment was Peter's sermon at Pentecost (Acts 2:36–37), when hearers were "pricked to the heart."

- **Enduring Word:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-16/
- **Ellicott:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/16.htm
- **Gill:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/john/16.htm

---

**v. 9 — "in regard to sin, because they do not believe in Me;"**

**Traditional Reading:** Commentators differ on whether "sin" here is unbelief specifically or sin generally with unbelief as its root. Ellicott argues it is "sin generally; unbelief in Christ is stated as the cause of sin" — sin is "missing the aim of life" because one has rejected the true centre of being, Christ. Morris (cited by Guzik) says: "The basic sin is the sin which puts self at the centre of things and consequently refused to believe in Him." Tenney says: "The essence of sin is unbelief, which is not simply a casual incredulity... rather, it is a total rejection of God's messenger and message." Gill sees the primary reference as the sin of the Jews in rejecting and crucifying Christ, which Peter charged them with at Pentecost.

- **Enduring Word:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-16/
- **Ellicott:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/16.htm
- **Gill:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/john/16.htm

---

**v. 10 — "in regard to righteousness, because I am going to the Father and you will no longer see Me;"**

**Traditional Reading:** "Righteousness" here is Christ's own righteousness, not that of the world. The ascension proves that Jesus fulfilled the Father's will perfectly — Heaven received Him, vindicating His righteousness against the world's verdict that He was a sinner (John 9:24) and a malefactor (John 18:30). Ellicott: "His return to the Father was Heaven's witness to His righteousness." Gill adds a soteriological dimension: the Spirit convinces believers of the insufficiency of their own righteousness and the necessity and sufficiency of Christ's imputed righteousness. The phrase "you will see Me no more" means they will no longer behold Him in His state of humiliation.

- **Enduring Word:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-16/
- **Ellicott:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/16.htm
- **Gill:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/john/16.htm

---

**v. 11 — "and in regard to judgment, because the prince of this world has been condemned."**

**Traditional Reading:** The judgment (*krisis*) of Satan at the cross (John 12:31) proves there will be a final reckoning. The perfect tense ("has been condemned") indicates an accomplished fact with ongoing results. Dods says: "The world, the prince of it, is 'judged'. To adhere to it rather than to Christ is to cling to a doomed cause, a sinking ship." Guzik notes that normally conviction is followed by judgment, but the Spirit inserts the revelation of Christ's righteousness between conviction of sin and warning of judgment — offering a way of escape through the righteousness of Another. Ellicott connects this to the opening of the Kingdom: "The power of the prince of this world is overcome by the opening of the kingdom of heaven to all believers."

- **Enduring Word:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-16/
- **Ellicott:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/16.htm
- **Gill:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/john/16.htm

**Denominational differences on vv. 8–11:** The main difference concerns *how* the Spirit convicts. Reformed teachers (Piper, MacArthur) emphasise the Spirit works *through the church's preaching of the Word*. Pentecostal/Charismatic teachers (Guzik, Enduring Word) acknowledge the Word but place stronger emphasis on the Spirit's *direct, experiential* convicting work — Guzik's commentary includes a long illustration from the 1860–61 British revival about the Spirit "opening men's eyes" in a terrifying, immediate way. The Baptist Garner-Howes commentary sees the Spirit's convicting work as operating "in and through the personal, physical, restricted presence of Christ" now made universal via the church. The older commentators (Gill, Ellicott) tend to blend both — the Spirit works through apostolic preaching but also directly on hearts. No major *doctrinal* dispute, but a difference in *emphasis*.

**Catholic/Orthodox note:** I was unable to retrieve specific Catholic or Orthodox sources for this chapter due to search limits. A search for *newadvent.org* or *catholic.com* on John 16 would be needed.

---

## vv. 12–15 — The Spirit's Work among the Disciples

**v. 12 — "I still have much to tell you, but you cannot yet bear to hear it."**

**Traditional Reading:** Jesus openly admits His teaching is incomplete — not because He lacks knowledge, but because the disciples lack capacity. The "many things" likely include the end of the ceremonial law, the full inclusion of Gentiles, and the nature of the New Covenant church. Ellicott notes this is a lesson for all teachers: "The fact that there were truths which Christ Himself could not teach is a lesson which men who profess to teach in Christ's name have too seldom learnt. St. Paul found in it a rule for his own practice" (feeding with milk, not meat; 1 Corinthians 3:3).

- **Enduring Word:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-16/
- **Ellicott:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/16.htm

---

**v. 13 — "However, when the Spirit of truth comes, He will guide you into all truth. For He will not speak on His own, but He will speak what He hears, and He will declare to you what is to come."**

**Traditional Reading:** "Into all the truth" (Greek has the article: *eis tēn alētheian pasan*) refers to the specific truth about Christ's person and work. Tasker says: "The New Testament is permanent evidence that the apostles were guided into truth about this." Guzik calls this "anticipation of the formation of the New Testament." The Spirit does not speak from Himself (*aph' heautou*) — just as the Son only spoke what He heard from the Father (John 8:28), the Spirit only speaks what He hears. "Things to come" includes both predictive prophecy (e.g., Revelation) and the unfolding of the new Christian dispensation.

Ellicott adds a beautiful picture: "The fulness of truth is for the disciples an unknown territory. They are spiritually as blind men, feeling after the truth... The Spirit of Truth will take them by the hand, and, step by step, as they have strength to follow, will guide them into the territory."

**Spurgeon on v. 13 (from studylight.org listing):** Spurgeon preached a sermon titled "The Holy Ghost The Great Teacher" (1855) on this verse, emphasising that the Spirit teaches believers by illuminating Scripture, not by giving new revelations beyond Scripture. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/john-16.html

**Major Denominational Difference — Continuationism vs. Cessationism:** This verse is a significant dividing line. **Pentecostal/Charismatic** traditions (Enduring Word represents a moderate charismatic position) see this as an ongoing promise — the Spirit continues to guide believers into truth today through prophetic words, impressions, and fresh illumination, though Guzik qualifies that this is "never in opposition to the Scripture." **Reformed/Baptist cessationists** (Spurgeon, MacArthur) tie the promise specifically to the apostolic age and the completion of the New Testament canon. Alford (cited by Guzik) states bluntly: "This verse is decisive against all additions and pretended revelations subsequent to and besides Christ; it is being the work of the Spirit to testify and to declare the THINGS OF CHRIST; not any thing new and beyond Him." The **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary** echoes this: the Spirit guided "certain believers and apostles to complete the Bible by inspiration of the Holy Spirit."

- **Enduring Word:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-16/
- **Ellicott:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/16.htm
- **Spurgeon (via StudyLight):** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/john-16.html

---

**v. 14 — "He will glorify Me by taking from what is Mine and disclosing it to you."**

**Traditional Reading:** The Spirit's core ministry is to glorify Christ, not Himself. Spurgeon preached "The Holy Spirit's Chief Office" (1888) on this verse, stressing that any supposed spiritual experience or revelation that does not magnify Jesus is not from the Holy Spirit. Ellicott adds: "This is the test of the Spirit, 'Every spirit that confesseth that Jesus Christ is come in the flesh is of God.'" The Spirit takes what belongs to Christ and "announces" or "discloses" it to believers — He is the Communicator, not the Originator.

- **Enduring Word:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-16/
- **Spurgeon (via StudyLight):** https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/spe/john-16.html
- **Ellicott:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/16.htm

---

**v. 15 — "Everything that belongs to the Father is Mine. That is why I said that the Spirit will take from what is Mine and disclose it to you."**

**Traditional Reading:** This verse grounds the Spirit's ministry in the unity of the Father and the Son. Clarke (cited by Guzik) asks pointedly: "If Christ had not been equal to God, could he have said this without blasphemy?" The verse implies the full deity of Christ and the Trinitarian harmony: the Father possesses all things; all the Father has belongs to the Son; the Spirit takes from the Son and reveals it to believers. Ellicott notes that verses 14–15 imply three doctrinal truths without stating them directly: (1) the divinity of the Son, (2) the personality of the Holy Spirit (*ekeinos*, "that one," used emphatically), (3) the Trinity in Unity.

- **Enduring Word:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-16/
- **Ellicott:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/16.htm

---

## vv. 16–18 — "A Little While"

**v. 16 — "In a little while you will see Me no more, and then after a little while you will see Me."**

**Traditional Reading:** The first "little while" refers to the few hours until Jesus' arrest and crucifixion; the second "little while" to the interval between His death and resurrection (three days). Trench (cited by Guzik) explains: "During the interval between His death and resurrection the disciples lost their faith and spiritual vision, and no more beheld Him than did the world." Then they "saw" Him with bodily eyes after the resurrection. Ellicott, however, suggests the second "seeing" extends to Pentecost — seeing Jesus in the Person of the Paraclete (cf. John 14:18–19), since John 16:23 connects "in that day" with the coming of the Spirit. The textual note: the phrase "because I go to the Father" is omitted from v. 16 in the best manuscripts (Ellicott).

- **Enduring Word:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-16/
- **Ellicott:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/16.htm

---

**vv. 17–18 — The disciples' perplexity:** Some disciples discuss among themselves, unable to understand the riddle of "a little while." The imperfect tense "they kept asking" (*elegon*) indicates an ongoing consultation (Tenney, cited by Guzik). They connect "a little while" with "because I go to the Father" (v. 10) and cannot reconcile the two.

- **Enduring Word:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-16/
- **Ellicott:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/16.htm

---

## vv. 19–22 — Sorrow Turned to Joy

**v. 19 —** Jesus, knowing their desire to question Him, repeats His saying to draw out their confusion.

**v. 20 — "Truly, truly, I tell you, you will weep and wail while the world rejoices. You will grieve, but your grief will turn to joy."**

**Traditional Reading:** Jesus predicts the disciples' deep grief at the crucifixion contrasted with the world's jubilation (the religious leaders' triumph, the mocking crowds). Yet this sorrow is not final — it "will turn to joy" (*eis charan genēsetai*). The world's joy is short-lived; the disciples' joy will be permanent.

- **Enduring Word:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-16/

---

**v. 21 — "A woman has pain in childbirth because her time has come; but when she brings forth her child, she forgets her anguish because of her joy that a child has been born into the world."**

**Traditional Reading:** The childbirth metaphor is a common Old Testament image for the transition from suffering to joy (Isaiah 26:17–19; 66:7–14). The "hour" of labour corresponds to the "hour" of Jesus' passion. The anguish is real and intense, but the joy that follows is so great that the pain is "forgotten" — not literally erased from memory but overshadowed and rendered insignificant by comparison. The "child" born is the new creation, the resurrection life of Christ and the birth of the Church.

- **Enduring Word:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-16/

---

**v. 22 — "So also you have sorrow now, but I will see you again and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take away your joy."**

**Traditional Reading:** The resurrection appearances are the immediate fulfilment ("I will see you again"). John Piper (Desiring God) emphasises that this joy is *indestructible* because it is rooted in the living Christ: "'I will see you again, and your hearts will rejoice, and no one will take your joy from you' (John 16:22). This indestructible joy is because 'I will see you again.' I will rise from the dead. I will be alive." The joy of Jesus' resurrection presence cannot be stolen by persecution, sorrow, or death.

- **Enduring Word:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-16/
- **Desiring God (Piper):** https://www.desiringgod.org/articles/no-one-will-take-your-joy-from-you

---

## vv. 23–24 — Prayer in Jesus' Name

**v. 23 — "In that day you will no longer ask Me anything. Truly, truly, I tell you, whatever you ask the Father in My name, He will give you."**

**Traditional Reading:** "In that day" refers to the post-resurrection, post-Pentecost age of the Spirit. "You will no longer ask Me anything" likely means they will be so overcome with joy at the resurrection that they will be speechless (Guzik), or that they will have direct access to the Father and will no longer need to ask Jesus as an intermediary in the same physical way. "Whatever you ask the Father in My name" is not a blank cheque — "in My name" means in alignment with Jesus' character, will, and purposes. Gill says asking in Jesus' name means "in the name of the Messiah, as though they believed in Him."

**Denominational note — Word of Faith / Prosperity teaching:** Some popular modern teachers interpret "whatever you ask" as an unconditional promise of material or physical provision if one exercises sufficient faith (the "name it and claim it" approach). However, none of the sources I retrieved directly address this controversy in their John 16 commentary. The traditional sources all qualify the promise by emphasising "in My name" as the controlling condition.

- **Enduring Word:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-16/
- **Gill:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/john/16.htm

---

**v. 24 — "Until now you have not asked for anything in My name. Ask and you will receive, so that your joy may be complete."**

**Traditional Reading:** Before Jesus' glorification, the disciples had not prayed "in Jesus' name" — they prayed to the God of Israel directly. Now a new era of prayer opens. The purpose of answered prayer is "that your joy may be complete" (*hina hē chara hymōn ē peplērōmenē*). This links back to John 15:11 and forward to the indestructible joy of v. 22.

- **Enduring Word:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-16/

---

## vv. 25–28 — Plain Speaking about the Father

**v. 25 — "I have spoken these things to you in figures of speech. An hour is coming when I will no longer speak to you this way, but will tell you plainly about the Father."**

**Traditional Reading:** "Figures of speech" (*paroimiais*, "proverbs" or "dark sayings") refers to the enigmatic nature of Jesus' Upper Room Discourse, including the "little while" saying and the vine imagery. The "hour" coming is the post-resurrection period, especially Pentecost, when the Spirit would illuminate their understanding. Gill says that after Pentecost the Spirit "should not only take of his things, but of his Father's also, and show them unto them clearly and plainly."

- **Enduring Word:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-16/
- **Gill:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/john/16.htm

---

**v. 26 — "In that day you will ask in My name. I am not saying that I will ask the Father on your behalf."**

**Traditional Reading:** Jesus is not denying His ongoing intercessory role (cf. Hebrews 7:25; Romans 8:34). Rather, He is emphasising that believers will have such direct, intimate access to the Father that they will not need Jesus to act as a go-between in the same way the disciples depended on His physical presence. The Father Himself loves them (v. 27). Gill explains: "I do not say that I will pray the Father for you; meaning that he would not only pray for them, but that the Father also loved them, and would hear them."

- **Enduring Word:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-16/
- **Gill:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/john/16.htm

---

**v. 27 — "For the Father Himself loves you, because you have loved Me and have believed that I came from God."**

**Traditional Reading:** The Father's love for believers is not earned by their love and faith; rather, their love for and faith in Jesus is the *evidence* that they belong to the Father and are the objects of His love. This remarkable statement grants believers the same intimacy with the Father that Jesus enjoys.

- **Enduring Word:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-16/

---

**v. 28 — "I came from the Father and entered the world. In turn, I will leave the world and go to the Father."**

**Traditional Reading:** Jesus summarises His entire mission in one verse: incarnation ("came from the Father"), earthly ministry ("entered the world"), death ("leave the world"), and ascension ("go to the Father"). This clear summary prompts the disciples' response in the next verse.

- **Enduring Word:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-16/
- **Ellicott:** https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/john/16.htm

---

## vv. 29–32 — The Disciples' Confession and Jesus' Reality Check

**v. 29–30 — "See, now You are speaking plainly and without figures of speech. Now we understand that You know all things... we believe that You came from God."**

**Traditional Reading:** The disciples perceive v. 28 as the "plain speaking" Jesus promised — it is a clear, linear summary. They profess faith and understanding. But their confidence is premature.

- **Enduring Word:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-16/

---

**v. 31 — "Do you finally believe?" Jesus replied.**

**Traditional Reading:** Jesus' question can be read as a statement (as in some translations: "Do you now believe?") — it is a gentle, sad challenge. Guzik: "He knew their faith would be shaken within hours when they fled and left Him alone." Their faith is real but fragile, and it is about to be tested as never before.

- **Enduring Word:** https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/john-16/

---

**v. 32 — "Look, an hour is coming and has already come when you will be scattered, each to his own home, and you will leave Me all alone. Yet I am not alone, because the Father is with Me."**

**Traditional Reading:** Jesus predicts the disciples' desertion, fulfilling Zechariah 13:7 ("Strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered"). "Each to his own" means each disciple will flee to his own concerns and safety. Yet even in total human abandonment, Jesus has the Father's presence — a comfort He extends to believers in v. 33. Gill notes that while the disciples would leave Him, "yet I am not alone, because the Father is with Me" — pointing to the unbroken fellowship within the Trinity even at the darkest hour.

## v. 33 — "I have told you these things so that in Me you may have peace. In the world you will have tribulation. But take courage; I have overcome the world!"

**Traditional Reading:** This is the triumphant conclusion of the entire Farewell Discourse (John 14–16). Guzik notes: "In a moment Jesus would pray for His disciples. Before He did, He summarized the purpose of the long talk." Peace is found *in Christ*, not in the absence of trouble. "In the world you will have tribulation" — this is a promise, not a possibility. Yet "take courage" (*tharseite*) because Christ has already won the decisive victory. Ellicott emphasises the perfect tense: "'I have Myself overcome the world.' He speaks of the assured victory as though it were already accomplished." The cross, though yet future, is as good as done — and with it, Satan's defeat, sin's payment, and the world's ultimate judgment.

Precept Austin quotes James Smith's devotional outline, noting seven promises in this chapter: the Comforter, guidance and teaching, Christ's coming again, answered prayer, Christ's intercession, peace, and victory. https://www.preceptaustin.org/john-16-commentary

Spurgeon (via Precept Austin) adds: "Your Lord tells you that you will not get to heaven without trials: 'In the world ye shall have tribulation.' And he tells you this that it may not surprise you when it comes."

## Summary of Key Denominational Differences

| Issue | Traditional/Reformed/Baptist | Pentecostal/Charismatic |
|-------|---------------------------|------------------------|
| **v. 13: "Guide into all truth"** | Tied to apostolic age and completion of the NT canon (Spurgeon, MacArthur, Alford) | Ongoing illumination; fresh revelation that never contradicts Scripture (Guzik and moderate charismatics) |
| **vv. 8–11: How the Spirit convicts** | Primarily through the preached Word and the church's witness (Piper) | Direct, experiential conviction alongside the Word, sometimes in revival contexts (Guzik) |
| **vv. 23–24: "Ask in My name"** | Prayer aligned with God's will; "in My name" is the controlling condition | Same essential meaning in traditional Pentecostal teaching; extreme Word of Faith views not represented in sources retrieved |
| **v. 7: Advantage of departure** | Emphasis on completed atonement enabling the Spirit's coming (Gill) | Emphasis on the Spirit's experiential presence being better than physical presence (Guzik) |
